title: Taking Sides
full_review:
"Taking Sides" (New Yorker) poses intriguing questions about an artist's political responsibility. Unfortunately, director Istvan Szabo's film offers little in the way of satisfying answers or absorbing drama.

Based on a true story, the failed film is set in post-World War II Berlin where famed German symphony conductor Wilhelm Furtwangler (Stellan Skarsgard) is being investigated by U.S. Maj. Steve Arnold (Harvey Keitel).

Keitel plays Arnold as the ugly American determined to nail Furtwangler as a member of the Nazi Party at any cost, despite possible evidence to the contrary. Furtwangler is a bundle of contradictions, embodying the knotty issue of cultural freedom and political dominance: He saved Jewish lives while receiving Hitler's praises -- and the fringe benefits that accompanied them.

Lush, atmospheric settings cannot compensate for the circular dialogue that is unable to engage the viewer or push the story forward in any meaningful way. The one-note characters become talking heads in a script that doesn't fulfill its potential to make thoughtful comments on the power of government over cultural values. However, a worse problem is Szabo's inability to rein in Keitel. Keitel is a grating brute as the self-righteous officer who barks out his accusations. In contrast, Skarsgard's disquieted demeanor is conveyed with controlled, pained looks, alternately confused, then sorrowful and repentant.

Lacking dramatic tension, "Taking Sides" disappoints with its tentative tone and low-key energy.

Because of horrific depictions of mass graves and some rough language, profanity and crass expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
